correctness.rationale: A Ritt power \(T^N\) is power bounded, hence so is \(T\). Spectral mapping then forces every peripheral point of \(T\) to be an \(N\)-th root of unity, making the least common multiple \(d\) finite and necessary for every Ritt exponent. For sufficiency, set \(S=T^d\) and \(a=N/d\). The only possible peripheral point of \(S\) is \(1\), so \(Q_a(z)=1+z+\cdots+z^{a-1}\) has no zero on \(\sigma(S)\) and \(Q_a(S)\) is invertible. The identity \(I-S^a=(I-S)Q_a(S)\) transfers the discrete derivative estimate from the Ritt operator \(S^a\) to \(S\). Positive powers of a Ritt operator are Ritt by a finite telescoping argument. This proves necessity and sufficiency, including \(d=1\).
correctness.risk: The proof assumes complex spectrum and existence of at least one Ritt power; it gives no existence criterion when no such power is known.

This is a natural reusable structural completion of the power question rather than a routine estimate.

final_claim: If one positive power of a bounded operator on a complex Banach space is Ritt, then the set of all Ritt exponents is exactly the positive multiples of the least common multiple of the orders of its peripheral spectral points, with the empty peripheral spectrum giving exponent one; in particular the Ritt exponents are closed under greatest common divisors.
limitations: The theorem is for complex Banach spaces and assumes at least one Ritt power exists.
The recent Badea paper remained full-text inaccessible in this run, so its exact internal theorem scope is a residual originality risk.
